articles.title: Big Buck's: Paul Nicholls pays tribute as legendary stayer dies aged 23
articles.summary: Paul Nicholls has paid tribute to his "invincible" hurdler Big Buck's, who has passed away at the age of 23; The Ditcheat horse, owned by the late Andy Stewart, won four consecutive Stayers' Hurdle crowns from 2009 to 2012.
articles.body:
Big Buck’s, one of the greatest staying hurdlers of all time, has died at the age of 23.

Owned by the late Andy Stewart, he was part of a golden age for trainer Paul Nicholls as he counted Kauto Star, Denman, Master Minded and Neptune Collonges among his stablemates.

Big Buck's had always been viewed by connections as a potential top-class chaser, however, a fall at the final fence in the 2008 Hennessy Gold Cup saw him revert back to hurdles and he never looked back.

He won what is now the Stayers' Hurdle a record four times, the Liverpool Hurdle four times and three times he came home in front in the Long Walk Hurdle.

Big Buck's, who struck up a great relationship with Ruby Walsh, was a fan favourite as he would often hit a flat spot in his races before powering to victory.

Nicholls told the Press Association: "Ability-wise he was probably as good as anything I've ever trained, it's just a shame he couldn't jump a chase fence.

"He was a wonderful horse for a wonderful owner who deserved to own a great horse like that. Andy enjoyed the whole journey and shared it with everybody.

"The horse had a brilliant life and had a great time with us and then a great time with Mike and Lucy Felton in retirement, but sadly time caught up with him.

"I was very lucky to have him at the same time as Kauto Star, Neptune Collonges, Master Minded and Denman. He was definitely as good as any of them."

One of the last surviving members of that halcyon period for the Ditcheat handler, Big Buck's would go on to pass Sir Ken and win a then record 18 straight National Hunt races when reverting to hurdles, an achievement only eclipsed by Altior since.

However, for Nicholls there will always be the question of how high he could have climbed if remaining over the larger obstacles.

"He won the Graded race at Aintree over fences, jumped 18 fences and jumped them 18 different ways and still won," said Nicholls.

"It made me think he was a certainty in the Hennessy and he was unlucky that day, but he just wasn't a natural jumper of a fence.

"If Kauto Star hadn't been about at that time then we probably would persevered over fences and he had the ability to win a Gold Cup. If he had won the Hennessy that day it would have definitely given us a headache and it would have been interesting where he would have ended up.

"But over hurdles he was invincible. Andy said I was bonkers, but going back over hurdles was the best thing we ever did. History tells you how good he was and Cheltenham, Aintree, Newbury, Ascot - if there was a big staying hurdle race, he won them all - all those Grade Ones on the trot, what a horse."

Big Bucks would become a standing dish on Thursdays at the Cheltenham Festival, with his famous flat spot often sparking nervous gasps from supporters before hitting top gear and surging up the Cheltenham hill under Walsh.

When asked to nominate just one race in Big Bucks' decorated career littered with so many great triumphs it was his fourth-straight success in the day three feature, when seeing off arguably the deepest field he met, edging out Irish raider Voler La Vedette, that Nicholls remembers most fondly.

"His fourth World Hurdle was the one that sticks out as being very special," said Nicholls.

"But we had so many great days with such a brilliant horse and we were all very lucky to be associated with him."

articles.title: Shergar Cup: Ryan Moore helps Great Britain and Ireland to Ascot crown
articles.summary: Alongside team-mates Saffie Osborne and Dylan Browne McMonagle, Ryan Moore produced two inspired rides to clinch the Dubai Duty Free Shergar Cup, as well as the prestigious SIlver Saddle Trophy for himself at Ascot; Having won the first two races, Team Hong Kong finished second.
articles.body:
Ryan Moore bagged a Shergar Cup double on his return to the competition following a 20-year absence to help his Great Britain and Ireland team win the team event while he was also crowned leading rider over the six races.

Winner of the Silver Saddle on his last appearance at the team-based meeting in 2006, Moore has usually been required to ride on a Group One card in Ireland.

But with that meeting put back 24 hours he was free to attend and delighted the Ascot crowd.

Team Great Britain and Ireland topped the standings on 81 points from Team Hong Kong in second on 62, with Moore's individual haul of 47 enough to take the Silver Saddle.

  • Nicholls pays tribute as Big Buck's dies aged 23
  • Blue Bolt confirms superiority over Precise at Deauville

He first struck on Dylan Cunha's Asgard's Captain (13-2) who stuck to his task gamely to win the Dubai Duty Free Shergar Cup Challenge by a length and a quarter from Yutake Take on Sportingsilvermine for the Rest of the World.

Moore said: "Dylan did say he could be a little bit lazy, but he has an uncomplicated attitude and to just help him through it and it was straightforward, really.

"It's great to get Dylan a winner here today and the owners will be delighted as they were all looking forward to it, so it's a good job the horse has performed today."

In the penultimate Dubai Duty Free Shergar Cup Classic, he gave Marco Botti's Archers Bay (5-2) a textbook ride coming home three-and-a-quarter lengths clear of Christophe Lemaire on King Of Berkshire for Team Europe.

Having run in the Italian Derby earlier in the season, he looked the class act and so it proved.

In the closing Dubai Duty Free Shergar Cup Mile, Moore finished third on Ozat behind the Frida Valle Skar-ridden Crown Board (10-1), but her Team Europe were not in contention for top honours by then.

Saffie Osborne thrives in the team environment and got her name on the scoresheet when Tim Easterby's Red Spells Danger justified 2-1 favouritism in the Dubai Duty Free Shergar Cup Sprint.

Osborne was leading rider in the Racing League on three occasions and is captaining Moore and Dylan Browne McMonagle in Team Great Britain and Ireland.

She said: "I heard a few people knocking this horse today but I thought the track would really suit and it has. I'm just glad I pulled my finger out.

"Looking at the standard of jockeys here today, it's amazing - look at our team with Ryan Moore and Ireland's champion jockey.

"The win for me today is that I made Ryan laugh a couple of times, so I'm quite happy with that!"

Team Hong Kong had earlier set the pace winning the first two races.

Jerry Chau gave them the perfect start when partnering Tuco Salamanca to a clear-cut victory in the Dubai Duty Free Shergar Cup Dash.

Representing a team making its Shergar Cup debut, Chau, 26, gave Ollie Sangster's four-year-old the perfect ride, taking a lead into the final furlong before a gap opened up seamlessly.

Tuco Salamanca (4-1) quickened impressively to beat Gold Star Hero, ridden by Chau's team-mate Vincent Ho, by a length and a half.

Fandom and Suraj Narredu were third for the Rest of the World.

Chau told Sky Sports Racing: "It felt amazing when I hit the line.

"No words can describe riding a winner at Ascot. I grew up watching Ryan Moore on YouTube. I watched him as much as I could."

Luke Ferraris did not have to wait long to play his part for Team Hong Kong as after an opening race one-two from his team-mates, he drove home Dancing In Paris to win the Dubai Duty Free Shergar Cup Stayers.

Riding the Ian Williams-trained 17-2 shot, Ferraris came with a late run to collar Moore on Andrew Balding's Shrimp Shady to win by a length.

Mountain Road was third for Yutake Take and the Rest of the World.

Ferraris said: "That's phenomenal, he's a lot fitter than me! He was turned out in great order.

"He didn't settle as good as he should have, but he still produced a great turn of foot.

"I think I've only ridden in one two-mile race in recent years, so it was a bit of a change.

"We've a good group of young riders representing Hong Kong, so let's hope it continues."

articles.title: 'Exciting' Sun Goddess looks the part for record-breaking Aidan O'Brien in Phoenix Stakes at the Curragh
articles.summary: Aidan O'Brien enhanced his record-breaking tally in the Phoenix Stakes to 18 on Sunday as his 'very special' filly Sun Goddess gained a first success at the top level in the hands of Ryan Moore.
articles.body:
Sun Goddess came from last to first to provide Aidan O’Brien with his 18th win in the Keeneland Phoenix Stakes at the Curragh.

Johannesburg (2001), George Washington (2005), Holy Roman Emperor (2006) and Caravaggio (2016) are just a few of the big names to have won this Group One prize over the years and Sun Goddess was the 5-4 favourite to add to that tally under Ryan Moore.

The daughter of Sioux Nation - who also won this race for the same connections in 2017 - had won each of her two previous starts over the course and distance, including a Group Two on her latest outing, with a runner-up finish behind George Boughey's Libertango in the Albany Stakes at Royal Ascot sandwiched in between.

With stablemate Carry The Flag setting a furious early pace, Moore was content to bide his time aboard Sun Goddess, but she came through stylishly on the far side of the track, racing inside the final two furlongs and was well on top as she passed the post a length and a quarter clear of Folsom Blues.

  • Blue Bolt confirms superiority over Precise at Deauville
  • Crowley 'looking forward' to kickstarting training career

O'Brien said: "She's a beautiful filly. She ran well at Naas the first day then came back here to win her maiden and then she went to Ascot probably a little under par, with the benefit of hindsight.

"Then she came back here a week after and won even though she was in Ascot the week before. She's obviously very special and everything went really well since Ascot."

He added: "She has a lot of gears and a very high cruising pace. Ryan said they went fast and he just said when he started to ask her she motored clear. He said she'll have no problem getting seven furlongs. She's very exciting."

Big Mojo bounces back to winning ways at the Curragh

Big Mojo made the most of having his sights lowered with victory in the FBD Hotels And Resorts Phoenix Sprint Stakes at the Curragh.

Mick Appleby's colt showed his worth at the highest level last season, winning the Sprint Cup at Haydock as well as finishing a neck second to No Half Measures in the July Cup at Newmarket.

The four-year-old has struggled so far this year, finishing down the field at York, Royal Ascot and on his second attempt at July Cup glory last month, but he had less on his plate in Ireland and stamped his class with a one-and-a-quarter-length verdict over Bucanero Fuerte under Tom Marquand.

A return to Haydock looks to be on the agenda, as does the Breeders' Cup, and Appleby, saddling his first winner on Irish soil, said of the 5-4 favourite: "He's done it well. We brought him here just to give him a bit more confidence, really. I think he was just lacking a bit in confidence with the big races he's run in.

"Now that he's got his head back in front hopefully he'll go and do it again. He's as good as ever. He's just got a bit more laid-back, like me! It's hard to win these races.

"There are a lot of good sprinters about. He's done it well enough. He only did what he wanted to do. There's a lot more there."

Michael O'Callaghan is confident Push The Boat Out can make his mark at a higher level following his successful debut in the Follow Us On Instagram @ GuidenstownStud Irish EBF Maiden.

Although not that well fancied in the market at 16-1, the Kodi Bear colt quickened smartly to record a comfortable victory under Colin Keane and it came as no surprise to his trainer.

O'Callaghan said: "He's a horse we've held in high regard from the moment we got him, but saying that I did have him slightly undercooked because he's very natural at home.

"He jumped and travelled with a lot of natural pace and quickened up well. Colin was quite taken by him and said he should have no problem stepping up into stakes company.

"I don't think he'll have any problem going another furlong and I think he could be a high-class stakes horse. We'll see how he is in the morning and see what there is between now and the National Stakes and go from there."

Aidan O'Brien's Ibelieveicanfly (13-8 favourite) opened her account at the fourth attempt in the Grand Hotel Malahide Irish EBF Fillies Juvenile Race.

Fourth, second and fourth in her first three races, the daughter of Frankel was fitted with a hood for her latest assignment and came good in some style, rewarding her supporters with a dominant five-length win in the hands of Ryan Moore.

"The better the race, the better she is going to be - she has such a high cruising pace," said O'Brien.

"In an ordinary run maiden, she is just in a gear too high. She has a lot of class. There was plenty of pace on and Ryan was very happy with her."

O'Brien and Moore doubled up in the Guidenstown Stud Irish European Breeders Fund Maiden with 8-15 favourite Shakespeare.

The son of Dubawi had shown a good level of ability with placed efforts on his first two starts and duly made it third time lucky without too much fuss.

O'Brien added: "He's a lovely big horse who does everything right. He's a little bit of a baby. That's why it took two runs for him to get to where he is.

"He's still not there. He has a lot of ability and is in the 'could be anything' category, really.

"Size, power, quality, speed, stamina - he has everything. Hopefully he's going to be something to look forward to."

"He's still not there. He has a lot of ability and is in the 'could be anything' category, really.

"Size, power, quality, speed, stamina - he has everything. Hopefully he's going to be something to look forward to."

articles.title: Samangan stars in Prix Maurice de Gheest
articles.summary: Francis-Henri Graffard took the headlines again in Deauville as the Aga Khan Studs-owned Samangan gained a first success at the top level in the Prix Maurice de Gheest.
articles.body:
Samangan gave Francis-Henri Graffard another Group One success with victory in the ARC Prix Maurice de Gheest at Deauville.

Always close to the pace-setting Afandy over the intermediate six-and-a-half-furlong trip, the Aga Khan Studs-owned Samangan battled through the final quarter-mile to master Stolen Kiss and just found the post coming in time to foil the William Haggas-trained Division, who flashed home under James Doyle.

The winner had been fourth in the Prix Jean Prat last time out in which True Love was second, but comprehensively reversed form with the Ballydoyle Classic heroine on this occasion.

Nemone Routh, racing manager for the owners in France, told Sky Sports Racing: "He's a lovely horse, he's very genuine. He was always going to follow Afandy and then he was really brave.

"He could (go to Ascot on Champions Day), but I think he's better on good, firm ground, that's another thing we've found this year. I think if it got too soft he wouldn't go there. He's a relaxed horse and he can get seven (furlongs). It all depends on the ground."

Graffard added: "I am very pleased for the stable. He is a colt we have always held in high regard. Things did not go as planned at the beginning of the season, but he also needed to gain experience.

"His previous races have toughened him up and this victory is the result of the experience he has been able to acquire.

"His next target could be the Qatar Prix de la Foret, provided the ground is not too testing for him. He is a Group One winner and exceptionally well bred, so he has earned his place at stud as a stallion. My job is done!"

Distant Storm boosted star three-year-old milers Bow Echo and Gstaad as he made a winning reappearance in the Prix Daphnis.

Third to Bow Echo in the 2000 Guineas at Newmarket before finding only Gstaad too good in the Irish equivalent, Charlie Appleby's colt had been off since that run at the Curragh.

Returning to the track in Group Three company, Billy Loughnane's mount was a little tight for room before getting out to give chase to well-backed Italian raider Grand Son Of Dark.

The Godolphin runner had a fair bit to do but always gave the impression he would get there and he duly did, to set up a return to bigger and better things.

Loughnane said: "I ended up a little further back than ideal, but the pace was even which was ideal and when I popped him out the top of the straight he had a target to run at.

"He's a horse that doesn't do too much when he's there, so having a horse to aim at was good and he won cosily in the end. He's horse that has a nice turn of foot, he takes a bit of time to pick up but when he does he's electric through the line.

"I was pretty confident I had everything covered."

articles.title: Weekend Winners: Rayif fancied to take Prix Jacques Le Marois prize at Deauville
articles.summary: Ahead of a busy weekend of action domestically and on the continent, the Weekend Winners trio of Kate Tracey, Declan Rix and Sam Boswell return to preview racing from Newbury, Ripon and Deauville; Watch the episode on the At The Races YouTube channel.
articles.body:
On the latest episode of Weekend Winners, the panel took an in-depth look into Sunday's Aga Khan Studs Prix Jacques Le Marois from Deauville.

Despite defeat at the hands of Blue Bolt last time, Aidan O'Brien's Precise heads the betting for the Group 1 showdown for three-year-olds and over. The yard won the race with Diego Velazquez last term and will be confident of another success here, with Ryan Moore booked to ride.

The British contingent are represented by Zeus Olympios and More Thunder, whilst Sixpence and Strauss fly the flag for Japan. In terms of the home side, Rayif holds strong claims for Francis-Henri Graffard after victory in the French 2000 Guineas earlier in the season.

Declan Rix...

"I'm liking the Francis Henri Graffard-trained Rayif, who will be happier back at a mile than last time [when fifth in the Prix Jean Prat over seven furlongs]. He won the French 2000 Guineas impressively with cut under foot and if he bounces back, on that run he will be a dangerous challenger.

"The drop to seven behind Thesecretadversary was a good run, given he had a setback going into Royal Ascot. He wasn't ideally placed in the race and ran on well and I think there is plenty of pace on offer here. He can sit and stalk the leaders and is overpriced against the older horses here.

Kate Tracey...

"I am with Rayif as well here. I'm hoping he can bounce back to his French 2000 Guineas form. Last time it all went wrong - he was down in trip and in the wrong position. I am hoping he can build on that.

"This is the first race he has had this season in which he has had this target, without any interruptions this time. The surface is quick - which is the opposite of his Guineas win - but connections have said they are wanting better ground so this should be in his favour."

Sam Boswell…

"I thought Precise was interesting in here. She has been a typical Aidan O'Brien three-year-old filly who is battle-hardened and was campaigned strongly this year. We saw her run at Deauville behind Blue Bolt in the Prix Rothschild, which she ran creditably in.

"My only concern is the quick turnarounds repeatedly, which it is for her even though she has shown she is good enough to compete at this level. I think she could get the Group One against the boys here."

Watch Weekend Winners in full on the At The Races YouTube channel...

articles.title: Dutch GP 2026 Sprint weekend dates, schedule, weather, UK start time and how to watch or stream F1 race at Zandvoort live on Sky Sports
articles.summary: Find out the race-day schedule, weather and how to watch the Dutch Grand Prix Sprint weekend at Zandvoort; watch the Dutch Grand Prix on Sunday at 2pm (build-up from 12.30pm), live on Sky Sports F1
articles.body:
Formula 1 is back after its summer break as the second half of the 2026 season begins with a Sprint weekend at the Dutch Grand Prix.

This is also the last Dutch Grand Prix as the event has not been renewed beyond this year, so the Orange Army will be out to support Max Verstappen racing on home soil for potentially the final time in his career.

Verstappen is yet to win a race this year but could play a key role in the title race as Kimi Antonelli looks to remain in control of the Drivers' Championship.

  • F1 2026 standings | F1 2026 calendar | F1 Gossip Column
  • Download the Sky Sports app for expert analysis, best video & more📱
  • Not got Sky? Get Sky Sports or stream with no contract on NOW📺

Antonelli leads Lewis Hamilton by 50 points and George Russell by 59 points but that advantage could quickly disappear, particularly if Ferrari continue to bring upgrades.

On paper, the Zandvoort circuit should suit Ferrari as it does not feature many straights but McLaren's Lando Norris won last time out at the twisty Hungaroring and should also be a threat.

Oscar Piastri won last year's Dutch Grand Prix, which is currently his last victory in F1, and the Australian needs to rediscover that form again in the second half of this season.

It is also a big race for Russell, who got engaged to his long-term partner Carmen Montero Mundt over the summer break, given Antonelli's superb recent form.

Dutch GP circuit: Zandvoort track layout

Zandvoort is one of the drivers' favourite tracks thanks to its high-speed corners and banked bends at Turn 3 and the flat-out final turn.

It can be tricky to overtake with only one long straight down to Turn 1 so track position is critical and we could see a similar race to Hungary last time out.

Dutch GP weather at Zandvoort

Despite rain threatening throughout the weekend, it is set to be a dry race albeit cold - with temperatures only reaching 20C.

articles.title: Godolphin's Gold Cup hero Trawlerman retired
articles.summary: John Gosden announced the news that Godolphin's staying star Trawlerman has been forced into retirement on Saturday, having picked up a leg issue after his run in the Goodwood Cup.
articles.body:
Trawlerman, winner of the Gold Cup at Ascot last year, has been retired after picking up an injury at Goodwood.

The eight-year-old, who won over £2m in prize-money, also won the Long Distance Cup on Champions Day twice and an Ebor.

Trained by John and Thady Gosden, he returned from an eight-month lay off to run a tremendous race in this year's Gold Cup, pushing his much younger rival Scandinavia all the way before succumbing by just a head.

He took on that same rival again but in an unsatisfactory race where he was hampered by a loose horse, he was beaten a long way.

  • Unbeaten star Bow Echo in shock retirement after setback
  • 'Exciting' Sun Goddess looks the part in Phoenix Stakes

Just this year the Gosdens realised he had a condition in his eyes that made them very sensitive to sunlight and he has been wearing ski goggles to protect them from the sun.

"Trawlerman is happy and well, but unfortunately he came out of the Goodwood Cup with a leg issue and is now being retired," John Gosden told www.godolphin.com.

"At eight years old, he has become part of the family here and won the Long Distance Cup twice and the Ascot Gold Cup in a very fast record time, which is unlikely to be equalled, as well as the Ebor.

"He has won over £2m in prize-money and remained at the top of his game this year when second in the Ascot Gold Cup, beaten a head giving 1lb to the winner.

"He will be retired to Wood Ditton Stud, where Godolphin have wonderful facilities that he knows well having been there for holiday.

"For all of us at Clarehaven Stables, just like Stradivarius, Trawlerman has become a much-loved member of the family and there are a lot of people here who will miss him particularly Ben de Paiva, who looks after him and Richard Wilkinson, who rode him through most of his career."

articles.title: Kevin Blake's Ebor Festival tips: Sky Sports Racing expert looks ahead to York's opening day with three selections
articles.summary: Day one of the York Ebor Festival takes place on Wednesday and is headlined by the Juddmonte International Stakes; Sky Sports Racing's Kevin Blake has put up three selections on the undercard on the Knavesmire
articles.body:
Kevin Blake has three picks for day one of the York Ebor Festival, an afternoon headlined by the Juddmonte International Stakes.

The Ebor Festival at York can make a game claim to be one of the very best four days of Flat racing anywhere in Europe. It is packed with quality stakes races and fiercely-competitive handicaps that present a great challenge no matter what your preferences. I'll do my best to pull a few winners from it in the coming days in this column....

The opening Hong Kong Jockey Club World Pool Handicap (1:50) starts this meeting off on Wednesday in devilishly-difficult style. Cases can be made across the track and while he has shortened up in price since the betting opened, I am sticking with the Richard Spencer-trained The Man.

Spencer is on track to have his best-ever year, and he is particularly good in these valuable sprint handicaps. The Man has shown a liking for this track, winning here in May 2025 and finishing an excellent head second in this race off 92 last year.

  • Rayif roars back to his best to land Prix Jacques le Marois
  • Godolphin's Gold Cup hero Trawlerman retired

A winter in Dubai didn't yield the riches it promised, but it would be no surprise at all if his connections have been targeting this meeting with him ever since he returned from his post-Dubai break. He has had two runs to blow away the cobwebs in the last seven weeks and shaped well on both occasions. He can be expected to be at fever pitch here and with the draw appealing as having been kind to him, a big effort should be forthcoming.

The Tattersalls Acomb Stakes (2:25) is the first of what will be a feast of two-year-old races at this meeting, and my preference is for the Ed Walker-trained Alfred Wallace. A son of Dubawi out of the wonderful race mare Snow Lantern, he is certainly bred to be smart. He showed plenty of promise when putting up a good figure in victory at Thirsk in May and shaped well for a long way before weakening late after forcing the pace in the Superlative Stakes at Newmarket.

Switched to an even stiffer seven furlongs in the Pat Eddery Stakes at Ascot, his connections opted to experiment with completely different tactics by dropping him in and riding with patience. The experiment proved to be a roaring success, as he overcame trouble in running to produce a fine winning effort. He could well be able to improve on that now that the key to him has been found and I expect him to run a big race.

My final selection of the day comes in another ridiculously competitive sprint handicap, the Irish Thoroughbred Marketing Handicap (4:45). It is worth taking a shot on the Michael Keady-trained Underwriter. The three-year-old might well prove to be one of the bargains of the season, as he was bought by current connections for just 4,600gns in a Tattersalls online sale at the beginning of July.

His first run for them only showed subtle promise, but his latest effort in a valuable sprint handicap at Ascot was notably eye-catching. Locked up and shuffled back to last in his group inside the final furlong, he flashed home in the final 100 yards and would have been third in another stride. That was very promising indeed and with the handicapper having dropped him quite aggressively from his high of 92, he looks a well-handicapped horse. If he can build on his Ascot effort, he will have a very serious chance.

articles.title: Hollie Doyle blog: Constitution River can come of age in Juddmonte International showdown with Ombudsman
articles.summary: Ombudsman and Constitution River set to do battle in thrilling Juddmonte International on day one of York's Ebor Festival; Doyle cheering on husband Tom Marquand aboard Maltese Cross in the Sky Bet Great Voltigeur Stakes
articles.body:
Sky Sports Racing ambassador Hollie Doyle runs the rule on day one of York's Ebor Festival on Wednesday, featuring the eagerly awaited clash between Ombudsman and Constitution River.

Aidan set for 8th success in mouthwatering Juddmonte

The remarkably versatile Ombudsman will be tough to deny in the £1.5m Juddmonte International Stakes (3.35), a stunning highlight on day one of the Ebor Festival at York on Wednesday.

John and Thady Gosden's five-year-old has added the Group 1 Dubai Turf in Meydan and the Prince of Wales' Stakes at Royal Ascot to his illustrious CV since taking this race in such spectacular style 12 months ago.

  • Kevin Blake's tips for opening day of York's Ebor Festival
  • Rayif wins the Prix Jacques Le Marois | Race replay

However, Aidan O'Brien's CONSTITUTION RIVER is something very special as he proved in the French Derby and the Coral-Eclipse and can come of age against his older rival in what promises to be an epic duel.

Two years younger and benefiting from that 7lb allowance, the son of Wootton Bassett hasn't yet reached his peak and is adaptable enough to lower the colours of Godolphin's superstar in what looks certain to be another tactical renewal.

Juddmonte's representative Item has proven his liking for this track with wins at Group 2 level in the Dante and the York Stakes but despite being only 2lb behind Constitution River on official ratings, needs to dig much deeper to usurp the main two.

Cross ready to stake Classic claim

MALTESE CROSS can stake his claim for the 250th running of the St Leger with a big performance in the Sky Bet Great Voltigeur Stakes (3.00) at York - a traditional trial for next month's final Classic.

My husband Tom (Marquand) is rightfully hopeful he can avenge his Derby defeat by Christmas Day in this 1m4f Group 2 after a hard-fought success in the Group 1 Grand Prix de Paris last month.

He'd have been an unlucky loser that day after overcoming all sorts of problems in running and should enjoy this galloping test on a sound surface on The Knavesmire before stepping up in trip at Doncaster.

Christmas Day couldn't repeat his Epsom heroics in the Irish Derby when his stablemate Pierre Bonnard finished only a neck behind him. In fact, I wouldn't be surprised to see that lovely colt emerge as the main Ballydoyle threat to Maltese Cross.

Haffner to frank strong Goodwood form

HAFFNER is the one they all have to beat in the Group 3 Tattersalls Acomb Stakes (2.25) at York despite finding one too good in the Vintage Stakes at Goodwood.

Aidan O'Brien's colt, who had previously won a Newmarket maiden, emerged with plenty of credit behind the unbeaten Dr Rascal on the Downs and has much less to prove than his rivals over this 7f.

If he under-performs, Ed Walker's talented colt Alfred Wallace could be the one to take advantage. The son of top-class race mare Snow Lantern gained a deserved success in a Listed contest at Ascot last time and can find the necessary improvement to go well in this better grade.

Madera can avenge unlucky run in Stewards' Cup

The big sprint handicaps at York are notoriously difficult to solve but I can make a strong case for TOCA MADERA in the opening Hong Kong Jockey Club World Pool Handicap (1.50).

David O'Meara's gelding would have gone much closer in the Stewards' Cup at Goodwood with a clear run and has been given the chance to gain compensation off an unchanged mark with stable jockey Danny Tudhope back on board.

I'm pleased to see him drawn low in stall four as I think that's the best place to be on the straight track, which we know plays to the strengths of the well supported The Man. Richard Spencer's runner was second in this last year but was well behind Toca Madera at Goodwood last month.

A better alternative at a bigger price may be Lemos de Souza's gelding Naana's Sparkle who finished in front of them both in that Goodwood sprint and will hopefully get a good tow into the race from his middle draw at rewarding odds.

Big chance for unlucky Small Fry

I nominated SMALL FRY as my 'Hot Shot' in this blog after his luckless run at the Goodwood Festival so won't be forsaking him in the Sky Bet Stayers Handicap (4.10) at York.

Joseph O'Brien's gelding got shuffled back at an important stage of the valuable Summer Handicap but still powered home to be a close second over 1m6f and can gain compensation despite a 4lb rise.

The step up to 2m can only be a positive for Joseph's son of Harzand who stays well and for the first time has the assistance of Ireland's champion jockey Dylan Browne McMonagle.

Andrew Balding's Shrimp Shady is becoming quite a force in top staying handicaps so don't rule him out either. He was second at the Shergar Cup after landing a big pot at Newbury at the expense of the likeable Team Player and will enjoy the test ahead of him on The Knavesmire.

articles.title: Formula 1: Kimi Antonelli - the boy 'born in a garage' and made on the track
articles.summary: Kimi Antonelli was a natural driver at the age of three, according to his dad. Here's how he went on to lead the F1 drivers' championship at the age of 19.
articles.body:
Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.

The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.

It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"

Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.

"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.

"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.

"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.

"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"

Now a 19-year-old Kimi is dominating this year's F1 championship in only his second season.

This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".

"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.

It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.

"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.

Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.

"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.

"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"

Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.

"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.

In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.

He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.

"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."

Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.

The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.

Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.

But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he got into, he was quick, and won.

By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.

It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.

"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."

Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.

Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.

"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.

At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.

This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.

By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.

So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.

Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.

Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".

"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'

"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"

Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.

"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.

"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."

Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.

Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.

"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.

"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.

"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.

"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.

"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."

Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.

It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.

Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.

"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."

Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.

Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.

"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.

There were stand-out moments, including pole for the sprint in Miami.

But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.

"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.

Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.

"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."

Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".

"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."

A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.

"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"

Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".

"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."

Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.

"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.

"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."

Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He has taken the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.

In the best car in the field, Antonelli has taken six poles and six wins in 11 races and heads into the second half of the season, starting at the Dutch Grand Prix this weekend, with a 50-point lead in the championship, and well on course for his first world title. If it had not been for dodgy reliability, he could be even further ahead.

The extent of this turnaround has shocked almost everyone.

"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.

"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."

Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.

"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.

"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."

Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.

"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."

Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".

"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."

Antonelli-Russell contrast could hardly be more stark Published 7 June

Antonelli-Russell contrast could hardly be more stark

Antonelli says he still has questions to answer Published 11 June

Antonelli says he still has questions to answer

Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.

Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"

The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.

Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not [fitting the stereotype of] a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'

"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."

Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.

"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.

"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."

Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.

"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says.

"We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."

Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.

"Toto said 'Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1'," Marco says.

"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He has taken the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.

In the best car in the field, Antonelli has taken six poles and six wins in 11 races and heads into the second half of the season, starting at the Dutch Grand Prix this weekend, with a 50-point lead in the championship, and well on course for his first world title. If it had not been for dodgy reliability, he could be even further ahead.
The extent of this turnaround has shocked almost everyone.

"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.

"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."
Antonelli-Russell contrast could hardly be more stark Published 7 June
Antonelli-Russell contrast could hardly be more stark
Antonelli says he still has questions to answer Published 11 June
Antonelli says he still has questions to answer

Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.

Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not [fitting the stereotype of] a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says.
"We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said 'Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1'," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

articles.title: Item surprises big two for Juddmonte International glory
articles.summary: We were treated to another epic renewal of the Juddmonte International on Wednesday but it was far from the match-race that it was built up to be, with Item delivered late to deny Almaqam in a thrilling finish to the York feature.
articles.body:
Item delivered for Andrew Balding and the sponsors to land a 10-1 surprise in the Juddmonte International at York – with the big two of Constitution River and Ombudsman only third and fourth respectively.

Hawk Mountain rather unexpectedly set the early pace, with stablemate Constitution River tucked in keenly behind him and odds-on favourite Ombudsman at the rear under William Buick, kept company by another Aidan O'Brien runner, Action.

Hawk Mountain was still in front as they moved to the top of the long Knavesmire straight, with Buick beginning to make headway on the inside rail, as Ryan Moore and Constitution River kicked for home over two furlongs out.

Ombudsman kept making ground on the inside, but the dangers were coming on the outside and it was Ed Walker's Almaqam who pulled away with half a furlong to run, only for Item to arrive in full flight, just getting his head down on the line in the hands of Colin Keane.

  • Item surprises big two for Juddmonte International glory
  • Godolphin's Gold Cup hero Trawlerman retired

Balding has now achieved something his later father, Ian, the trainer of Mill Reef, never managed. He said: "I don't think he had many goes at it, though, in fairness. It's always one of the most important races of the year. So it's lovely to win it with a horse like this.

"We've pitched him in some good races with the belief that he will do well in them, but he's kept improving and improved physically. That's the most important thing.

"He's really a very different horse than the one that ran in the Dante, physically."

He added: "I think anything is possible, he certainly has no problem staying a mile and a half if he wanted to.

"I just want to say a big thank you to the team at home because it wasn't straightforward getting him here. Everything had gone great up until about declaration time and we had a little hiccup there with his feet.

"Thankfully everyone who looks after him have worked overtime to get it right, and happily it was a 5am decision that he got on the box to come up here. I'm very relieved."

On Item's next assignment, the Kingsclere handler said: "I just do not know at this moment in time. I think we've got to sit down and let the dust settle. We've just won a Juddmonte International, that was the plan."

articles.title: Hollie Doyle: Kalpana can prove too hot for Yorkshire Oaks rivals
articles.summary: Kalpana is looking to back up her King George success in the Yorkshire Oaks on day two of York's Ebor Festival; Doyle believes Juddmonte Farms and Andrew Balding can make it two Group Ones in two days.
articles.body:
Our ambassador returns to preview the second day of the Ebor Festival at York on Thursday, covering a variety of Group, Handicap and Listed events.

Kalpana too hot for Minnie in Yorkshire Oaks

Kalpana, a brilliant winner of the King George last month, will prove too hot for Minnie Hauk to handle in Thursday's showstopper at York, the Group One Legends Global Yorkshire Oaks (3.35).

The great French horse Calandagan simply had no answer to Andrew Balding's mare at Ascot, where Aidan O'Brien's multiple Oaks winner finished a disappointing 18 lengths adrift.

That was the second time in a row Minnie Hauk has put in an underwhelming performance and I just can't see her re-capturing her best form in time to bridge that yawning gap. Back against her own sex, Kalpana is simply irresistible, even if the forecast rain arrives.

  • Rayif wins the Prix Jacques Le Marois | Race replay
  • Godolphin's Gold Cup hero Trawlerman retired

At bigger odds, I hope to see David Menuisier's Inis Mor maintain the progress that has seen her make the frame in both the French and Irish Oaks. This is tougher still, but Oisin Murphy knows how to get the best out of her.

Irish filly ready to step into Pattern company

Juddmonte's Irish-trained filly Livenka looks ready to stamp her class on the Group Two Sky Bet Lowther Stakes (1.50) at York on Thursday.

Ger Lyons' daughter of Bated Breath booked her place in this line-up by taking a valuable sales race at Naas by nearly four lengths, suggesting she's ready to step into Pattern company.

She's drawn high but isn't far away from the probable favourite Libertango, the Albany winner who only narrowly lost her unbeaten record in the Group Two Duchess Of Cambridge at Newmarket.

George Boughey's filly sets the standard, but Livenka arrives on an upward curve and looks too smart to ignore, while Andrew Balding's Moonrise is another big player. She was second in the Windsor Castle at Royal Ascot before winning the Princess Margaret yet has been largely overlooked in the Ante-post markets.

Oaks fourth stands out in Galtres

My husband Tom (Marquand) and his boss William Haggas can expect a big run from Rhapsody in the British EBF & Sir Henry Cecil Galtres Stakes (4.10) at York - but she has one filly in particular to be fearful of.

Rhapsody brings ideal credentials to this Listed race with a Group placing and a course win to her name. However, I'm expecting Ralph Backett's A La Prochaine to take full advantage of this drop-in class.

Still lightly raced, she ran well in the Cheshire Oaks in the spring but stepped forward again to be fourth in the Oaks itself at Epsom on her latest start. She's been freshened up since then and looks a much sounder proposition than the likely favourite Morrophore, who's best form has been achieved on the All-Weather. She must also overcome an eight-month absence.

Satellite the value in big sales dash

It's pretty unusual to see a Group One winner in a sales race but the participation of Sun Goddess in the Harry's Half Million By Goffs (2.25) at York demonstrates the limitless strength in depth at Ballydoyle.

Aidan O'Brien's Phoenix Stakes heroine looks thrown in on these terms and will probably go off an even shorter priced favourite if her Albany victor Libertango wins the Lowther.

Still, anything can happen in big-field sales races so there has to be some value in Clive Cox's unbeaten Satellite Of Love, who has over a stone to find with Sun Goddess but has a plum low draw and a progressive profile to go with it.

She really impressed me in her Newbury novice while I am also keeping an eye out for my boss Archie Watson's game filly Vollering, who has already picked up valuable black type in France and has plenty of experience now.

Bullet Point ready to follow up big Handicap

Bullet Point came back to form in timely fashion in this month's Shergar Cup and can go one better in the Sir Kevin Sinfield 7 In 7 Grand Finale Handicap (3.00) at York.

Last year's winner was clearly transformed by the first-time cheekpieces at Ascot and looks another winning chance for Tom (Marquand) if the headgear proves as effective a second time.

Ralph Beckett's Ante-post favourite Centigrade looks short enough for a horse stepping out of an All-Weather novice but I'd like to see Jack Channon's Mezcala involved at the business end of the race. The Buckingham Palace winner hasn't been blessed with the best of draws in stall 17 but will enjoy York if he gets that all-important luck in running.

Hollie Doyle was speaking to Sky Sports Racing's Simon Mapletoft.

articles.title: Kevin Blake's Ebor Festival tips: Sky Sports Racing expert looks ahead to day two at York with three selections
articles.summary: Day two of the York Ebor Festival takes place on Thursday and is headlined by the Yorkshire Oaks; Sky Sports Racing's Kevin Blake has put up three selections on the card on the Knavesmire
articles.body:
Sky Sports Racing’s Kevin Blake reveals a trio of picks as York's Ebor Festival rolls on into day two on Thursday.

The Ebor Festival at York rolls on into day two on Thursday and while the main events will provide world-class action for us to enjoy, it is the supporting card that might well offer the best betting opportunities.

The Sir Kevin Sinfield 7 In 7 Grand Finale Handicap (3:00) is yet another brutally-tough handicap puzzle to solve, but William Haggas may have the answer in the shape of BULLET POINT. The five-year-old won this race last year off a mark of 100, enjoying a smooth trip around from a good draw and winning with some authority.

  • Rayif roars back to his best to land Prix Jacques le Marois
  • Godolphin's Gold Cup hero Trawlerman retired

However, his career hasn't continued on the upward curve as might have been expected since then, with a trip down to Australia ending in disappointment followed by a six-month absence. Since his return, it wouldn't be at all surprising if his connections have been working backwards from this race.

He shaped with subtle promise in two runs in valuable handicaps earlier this season and then returned from another 12 weeks off to run a fine race in defeat at the Shergar Cup, finding just one that had got loose on the lead too good for him. He gets to run off the same mark of 101 here and while the draw hasn't been quite so good to him this year as it was last year, he still looks to have leading prospects.

The next contest of interest is the Mews Hotel Ossett EBF Stallions Nursery (4:45). Three weeks ago, this column put up the Hugo Palmer-trained MIA FANTASIA in a valuable nursery at Glorious Goodwood. To say he had a troubled passage would be underselling it! He got next to no luck in running and shaped much better than the bare result.

The case that made for him that day remains relevant, with him having overcome his inexperience to win in good style at Carlisle on debut before not quite being sharp enough to be as competitive in what has proven to be a smart novice contest at Ascot that was won by the subsequent Vintage Stakes winner Dr Rascal. A mark of 79 seems very fair indeed and he is sure to have benefited from the experience he gained at Goodwood. He looks likely to run a big race.

The final race of interest on the day is another very tough handicap, the British EBF Fillies' Handicap (5:20). Again, cases can be made for so many of these, but I'm going to venture down towards the bottom end of the weights and side with the Ed Walker-trained SECRET HISTORY.

The three-year-old has already won three times this year, with her most notable victory coming in a valuable seven-furlong handicap at Newmarket in July. Raised 4lb for that, her connections took a chance in dropping her to six furlongs to contest a valuable fillies' handicap at Glorious Goodwood and while she ran well to finish third, she shaped as though the test was sharper than ideal for her. Returning to this trip will be a big help to her and she looks to have very strong prospects.

articles.title: Max Verstappen: Red Bull driver signs new contract extension until 2030 Formula 1 season ahead of Dutch Grand Prix
articles.summary: Max Verstappen has signed a Red Bull contract that will see him stay at the team until at least the end of 2030; watch the Dutch Grand Prix Sprint weekend live on Sky Sports F1 from Friday with Practice at 11.30am and Sprint Qualifying at 3.30pm
articles.body:
Max Verstappen has signed a new long-term Red Bull contract until 2030 to end speculation over his future.

Verstappen's previous deal was due to expire at the end of 2028 and it is understood his management held talks with McLaren earlier this year over a switch for 2027.

The new contract will see him stay at Red Bull until at least the end of 2030 when Verstappen will be 33 years old.

  • Dutch GP: UK schedule and how to watch on Sky Sports
  • F1 2026 standings | F1 2026 calendar | F1 Gossip Column
  • Download the Sky Sports app for expert analysis, best video & more📱
  • Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺

The news almost certainly means there will be no driver changes at Formula 1's current top four teams - Mercedes, Ferrari, McLaren and Red Bull - for 2027.

"I am really pleased with the contract extension. We have the best people and I'm excited to keep working together with everyone to get back to the top again," said Verstappen, who is currently sixth in the Drivers' Championship and 110 points behind Kimi Antonelli ahead of this weekend's Dutch Grand Prix.

"This remains the ultimate goal that all of us have been working towards and will continue to pursue. I want to thank Red Bull, Laurent and everyone at Oracle Red Bull Racing for the trust they put in me.

"I have always said it: The team is like a second family for me and I feel very at home. I came to the team hoping to be able to win races. What we went on to achieve together has been simply lovely and we have shared many incredible moments and won four World Championships. To continue this journey with the same team that I have been with my whole career is really special and something I have always wanted to do.

"Getting to work with Laurent now for over a year has also been great, I see a clear vision he has for the team. Everyone in Milton Keynes believes in what we are building and I am looking forward to the next chapter, fighting for more victories and competing for championships as we continue to shape the future of this team."

Why has there been so much speculation about Verstappen's future?

Verstappen is widely regarded as the best driver in Formula 1 after winning four consecutive drivers' titles from 2021 to 2024 and coming within two points of a remarkable fifth championship in 2025 in inferior machinery compared to the two McLarens.

He expressed dissatisfaction at the new 2026 power unit regulations earlier this season, revealing in March that he was contemplating his future in the sport.

F1 has since tweaked the power unit rules, and further changes will be introduced to reduce the amount of electrical output for 2027 and beyond, and criticism over the yoyo style of racing has lessened as the season has gone on.

Red Bull also started the season poorly but have developed their way towards the front and appear to be getting on top of their reliability issues.

However, Verstappen had an exit clause in his contract that would allow him to join another team in 2027 as he was outside the top two positions in the Drivers' Championship at the start of this season's summer break earlier this month.

Despite having the possibility to leave, Verstappen has committed his future to Red Bull for another four and a half seasons.

    "Having Max continue with us and retaining the best driver on the grid is fantastic news for everyone at Red Bull, Oracle Red Bull Racing, as well as F1 and motorsport as a whole," said Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies.

    "Very few partnerships in sport achieve what Max and this team have. Since the very beginning, Max has embodied everything that makes Oracle Red Bull Racing special: uncompromising competitiveness, relentless determination and the courage to challenge convention.

    "His impact on our team and on Red Bull's motorsport story has been transformational, and he has been fundamental to everything we have accomplished together.

    "The decision to continue our journey together is rooted in the trust Max and the team have built over many years, as well as Max's confidence in our people, our culture and our vision for the future. Forged through championship-winning success, intense battles and challenging moments alike, this relationship has only grown stronger - making it one of Formula 1's greatest success stories.

    "But we are not done yet. There are more races to win, more milestones to achieve and more history to write. Together, we continue to raise the bar with the same determination that brought us to the top of the sport and an even greater faith in what we can achieve. Much will evolve as we move forward, but our ambition remains unchanged - united by one direction, one vision, one team."

    Why has Verstappen signed a new contract now?

    It is understood Verstappen had until October to tell Red Bull if he would remain at the team for next year but talks went well over the summer and the Dutchman has been convinced that he can win more races, and titles, at the Milton Keynes-based team.

    Red Bull have lost several key personnel in recent years including Christian Horner and Helmut Marko, while Verstappen's engineer Gianpiero Lambiase will join McLaren in 2028.

    But, Verstappen, who joined Red Bull in 2016, has seen enough progress this season and been shown Red Bull can challenge at the front in the future.

    Sky Sports F1's Karun Chandhok said: "Just look at the last two Grands Prix, he has had two podiums. Straight away the team has momentum.

    "That is what it was always going to take for Max to stay where he is. He wanted to see improvements.

    "Making their own engine at Red Bull is incredible stuff where you think where they have come from.

articles.body:
Max Verstappen said he came closer to retiring from Formula 1 than joining a rival team as he explained his reasons for extending his Red Bull contract.

In a relatively surprise announcement on the eve of his home Dutch Grand Prix, the first race back after the sport's summer break, Red Bull announced that Verstappen had extended his contract with them by two further years, to 2030.

The four-time world champion had been linked with Mercedes in each of the previous two years, while his management were understood to have spoken to McLaren. Verstappen had also called his whole F1 future into question earlier in the year with strong criticism of the sport's current engine rules.

  • Dutch GP: UK schedule and how to watch on Sky Sports
  • F1 2026 standings | F1 2026 calendar | F1 Gossip Column
  • Download the Sky Sports app for expert analysis, best video & more📱
  • Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺

Asked in a Red Bull press conference at Zandvoort following Thursday's announcement if he had been close to considering a future away from Red Bull, and whether there had been the chance to join a rival, Verstappen replied: "I think I was closer to retiring than changing teams!

"But, no, all good."

Asked directly in the later official drivers' press conference about the existence of any rival offers, Verstappen said: "It doesn't matter. It doesn't matter, does it? Well, not to me."

What changed for Verstappen to want to stay in F1 after rules complaints?

While Verstappen's previous contract at Red Bull ran to the end of the 2028 season, the deal was known to contain performance break clauses, while it had appeared in the new season's early weeks that the Dutchman might opt to walk away from the sport entirely due to dissatisfaction with the new-for-2026 power unit regulations which feature a near 50-50 split between between electrical and traditional internal combustion power.

But constructive talks between the sport's stakeholders, including drivers, led to early-season refinement of the regulations and an agreement to reduce the contribution of electrical power in 2027 and 2028.

Verstappen said on Thursday: "I have to say after the first few races I said to Laurent [Mekies, Red Bull's team principal], 'don't come to me with any kind of questions about the future, because I don't even know if I want to stay!'

"But honestly, we always kept it very open. I mean, I love racing and I think I had a lot of very good discussions with F1, but also with the FIA, and I think we are, let's say, slowly working towards something that becomes better and better.

"Also from my side, of course, you know, I adapted, I accept the situation that I think we're all in and just trying to make the best of that.

"I think also with the year that I signed to, it again opens up the door maybe when potentially the V8s come in to look at that again as well."

Verstappen was referring to the fact that 2030 could coincide with the first year of the sport's next engine formula, with a return to V8 engines - last used in the sport in 2013 - on sustainable fuels and with an element of electrification currently being explored.

He added: "It's what I said a bit before where I accepted kind of the situation that we're in. Personally, of course, I'm not happy with it but, at the same time, with the discussions that I've had with F1 and FIA already trying to make little improvements for next year or the year after.

"Plus, the year that I signed to - leaving the door open for a potential V8 return - I'm willing to accept that at the moment. It's, let's say, not fantastic but I still love racing.

"It's still a Formula 1 car. And some tracks [for energy deployment] are better than others. But, yeah, for sure, we know that in some areas I think we can improve. So, hopefully, over the years, it will get a little bit better."

'I never felt that desire or need to change to another team'

Verstappen and Red Bull have enjoyed stunning success in their decade together so far, with four drivers' titles from 2021-2024 and 71 race wins to establish themselves as one of F1's most decorated partnerships.

But the wholesale change in rules for this year has proved trickier so far, with just four podiums in 11 races, while Red Bull have appeared a team in transition over the past two years following a number of high-profile senior departures including Christian Horner, Adrian Newey and Helmut Marko.

Verstappen's long-standing race engineer, Gianpiero Lambiase, will also join McLaren by the start of the 2028 season.

But Verstappen said he had not felt the need to look for a different challenge elsewhere.

"A few names have left but, at the same time, it's still my family," said Verstappen, who was first signed by Red Bull to their junior programme as a 16-year-old in 2014.

"I never felt that desire or need to change to another team, to try and win somewhere else. If I feel well within the team here, why should I? Because I know that they do everything for me and they know that I do everything for them once I'm on the track and trying to get the results."

Verstappen's new deal will take him up to 15 seasons as a senior Red Bull driver and the 28-year-old quipped: "Practising for my own marriage! Just seeing how long I can eke that out in racing terms, and then try and triple that, at least, in marriage.

"I always said already, back in the day, when Dietrich (Mateschitz, team founder) was still alive, I said to him, my goal and target would be, of course, to race for Red Bull forever. So, we are on the good way."

Verstappen also batted away questions about whether, like his previous deal, there were break clauses in the latest contract.

"I mean, I've never disclosed anything in my contract," he replied. "So, yeah, that stays the same."
